source_reviews.independent_solution: An escaping surface molecule must do work against the attractive forces exerted by other liquid molecules. Separation increases intermolecular potential energy and requires sufficient kinetic energy; escaping is not simply motion through empty space with no energy cost. The task is to supply the physical work and the force opposed, not merely name evaporation.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The more energetic, faster-than-average molecules preferentially escape. The molecules remaining in the liquid consequently have lower mean kinetic energy, so their temperature falls when evaporation removes energy faster than external heat replenishes it. Work against cohesion also belongs in the energy account. A heat supply can maintain the temperature, so evaporation does not imply an unconditional temperature drop.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Construct a demonstration with two initially matched thermometers equilibrated in the same room. Put identical thin cotton coverings around their bulbs; wet one with room-temperature water and keep the comparison covering dry. Record the common initial reading, then expose both to the same airflow without contact or a heater and record the readings as the water evaporates. A fall of the wet bulb below its initial reading and below the dry comparison indicates evaporation takes energy from the bulb and covering. Initial water at room temperature and equal exposure rule out merely applying an initially cold liquid or changing room temperature as the explanation. The effect persists only when heat replacement is insufficient; strong heat replacement can suppress it. This uses water and does not require ether on skin or independent handling of a flammable volatile liquid.

The frozen independent solution constructed a water-based matched-control demonstration; this difference is not a contradiction. The source phenomena and experimental reasoning are present, while author limitations and coverage expressly defer independent design, setup, performance, readings and uncertainty. source_reviews.independent_solution: Different liquids have different strengths of intermolecular attraction. Under matched temperature, exposed area, airflow and surrounding-vapour conditions, stronger cohesion presents a larger escape-energy barrier, so fewer molecules can leave in the same time; weaker cohesion allows faster escape. In the seed's water/ether comparison, stronger water cohesion requires more work and gives slower evaporation than ether in the intended lesson model. This is an explanation using cohesion and escape energy, not a claim that identical temperature makes all molecular speeds identical or that molecular mass alone determines the rate.

mathematics.independent_solution: The molecular escape barrier comes from attraction by the other liquid molecules. An escaping molecule needs enough original kinetic energy to do separation work. The exact true set is C. Macroscopic pressure and gravity are not substitutes for that cohesive barrier; pressure or height equality cannot switch off intermolecular forces. Liquid molecules are already in thermal motion.

option_checks.evidence: Fixed air pressure does not eliminate attraction between liquid molecules. Even if pressure-related work can enter a macroscopic energy account, the compound statement replaces the molecular cohesive barrier and explicitly denies it; that denial is false. Author derivation comparison: The stated wrong procedure substitutes atmospheric pressure as the sole retention cause, then discards cohesion when that pressure is fixed. Those steps produce the full visible assertion, including its false denial of attraction; the derivation does not require claiming that all pressure-related work is impossible.

Putting the liquid at one height does not remove intermolecular attraction. A possible gravitational energy change is not the escape-work mechanism at the molecular surface, so the claimed irrelevance of cohesion is false. Author derivation comparison: The stated wrong procedure replaces molecular separation with macroscopic gravitational lifting and treats fixed container height as removing the relevant work. This generates the visible substitution and false irrelevance claim; attraction remains at fixed height.

Separating a surface molecule requires work against attraction by its neighbours; only a molecule with sufficient kinetic energy can complete escape in the seed model. mathematics.independent_solution: Preferential loss of high-kinetic-energy molecules lowers the mean kinetic energy of the population that remains. With no replacement of the evaporation energy, that decrease is cooling. The exact true set is A. Removing the slow class instead raises the remaining mean; merely reducing population size is not lowering temperature; increased mean kinetic energy cannot explain a lower temperature.

If slow molecules were removed from an ensemble with kinetic energies 1, 2 and 6, removing 1 raises the remaining mean from 3 to 4, not down. It also reverses which molecules can overcome the escape barrier. Author derivation comparison: The author explicitly derives this by selecting the slower departing group and then mistakenly assigning that group's low energy to the remaining group. The confused removed-versus-remaining procedure genuinely produces the claimed lower remaining mean; it is not a valid averaging calculation.

Removing each speed class in its original proportion leaves mean kinetic energy unchanged. For example, removing half of each class halves total energy and molecule count together, leaving energy per molecule and temperature unchanged in this proposed explanation. Author derivation comparison: Proportional removal first preserves the mean; substituting count or total energy for temperature then creates the false cooling conclusion. This is the exact two-step wrong procedure stated by the author and the visible option.

Removing a molecule with energy above the original mean lowers the remaining mean, not raises it. Increased mean kinetic energy would correspond to increased temperature, contradicting the proposed causal chain twice. Author derivation comparison: The author states two errors: departure of fast molecules is imagined to accelerate survivors, and increased motion is then interpreted as cooling. Together they produce both false clauses, consistent with the frozen above-average-removal and temperature-direction objections.
